papers.title: EXPRESS: How Gig Sellers Do the Hustle
papers.abstract: We conceptualize and develop theoretical insights related to a neglected category of market actors: gig sellers. Gig sellers are independent agents who sell products on behalf of a specific brand with marketing support. They face semi-entrepreneurial opportunities, meaning that while they are entirely responsible for managing the customer sales funnel, they do not develop new products or services like conventional entrepreneurs. They are compensated solely by sales commissions and do not receive salaries or benefits like organizational salesreps. Drawing on a large set of qualitative data from effective agents, we inductively and abductively draw inspiration both from literature and our analyses to unpack how these agents seize the opportunity to accomplish what is important to them. We find prominent reliance on effectual versus predictive practices is crucial to satisfactory achievement of outcomes. We expand our understanding of the range of outcomes that gig selling may result in, whether it be to remain in gig sales (enacting long-term loyalty, switching teams, or enriching) or enter alternative opportunity corridors (pursuing entrepreneurship, seeking employment). Our theoretical insights contrast with findings regarding salespeople in institutional settings and other categories of independent agents. Practical implications for agents and organizations are developed.

papers.title: EXPRESS: Slim Shading in Ad Auctions: Adjustment of Bidding Strategies to First-Price Rules
papers.abstract: We study how bidders adjusted to a switch from second-price to first-price auction rules on a large online advertising exchange. Under first-price rules, bidders should strategically reduce (“shade”) their bids. To assess whether observed bid reductions were sufficient given the competition each bidder faced, we develop a nonparametric estimator of a lower bound on the valuation underlying each bid. The estimator relies on localized measures of competition and does not require assumptions of bidder symmetry, valuation independence, or equilibrium bidding. Applying the method to more than 40 million auctions involving eight major demand-side platforms, we find pervasive insufficient bid shading after the switch. The implied lower bounds on valuations remain substantially above pre-switch levels for at least three months after the transition, indicating that none of the bidders we study shaded sufficiently. This finding is robust to alternative definitions of local competition, richer conditioning information, and variations in the assumptions underlying the estimator. The results suggest that adjustment to major auction-design changes can be surprisingly slow even among sophisticated algorithmic bidders, with implications for marketplace design and the interpretation of short-run “A/B test” experiments.

papers.title: Giving More in a Non-Native Language: The Effect of Language on Monetary Donations
papers.authors: Marie Ozanne, Archer Yue Pan, Xinlian Zhang, Kaitlin Woolley
papers.abstract:
Abstract
                  How does the language of a charitable appeal, whether communicated in a potential donor’s native or non-native (but proficient) language, influence monetary donations? Whereas research finds that people behave more morally in their native (vs. non-native) language, eight preregistered experiments (N = 7,447) and one archival analysis (N = 3,142) find that people donate less in response to appeals in their native language. People facing a donation decision need to determine whether and how much to give, with the appropriate action varying across situations. Situational considerations that inform this decision are more accessible in a native language, making donation decisions seem less diagnostic of the self, reducing giving. Consistent with this process, perceived self-diagnosticity mediates the effect of language on donations, and manipulating self-diagnosticity attenuates this effect. Reconciling these findings with prior research, the relationship between language and moral behavior depends on the type of moral decision under consideration: a native language promotes adherence to moral rules when decisions involve moral violations (stealing; lying), but reduces giving for donation decisions, which we refer to as moral aspirations. Beyond advancing theory on language, self-diagnosticity, and moral behavior, this research offers practical guidance to maximize charitable giving when communicating with multilingual audiences.

papers.title: EXPRESS: Causal Inference With Endogenous Price Response
papers.authors: Przemyslaw Jeziorski, Dingzhe Leng, Stephan Seiler
papers.abstract: The authors study the estimation of causal treatment effects on demand when treatment is randomly assigned but prices adjust in response to treatment. They show that regressions of demand on treatment or on treatment and price lead to biased estimates of the direct treatment effect. The sign of the bias in both cases depends on the sign of the correlation of price with treatment, and the two biases point in the same direction. In most cases including an endogenous price control reduces bias but does not remove it. The authors also show how to test whether bias from an endogenous price response arises and how to recover an unbiased direct treatment effect using a price instrument. They apply the approach to the estimation of feature advertising effects across several product categories using supermarket scanner data and show that the bias when not instrumenting price can be substantial.

papers.title: EXPRESS: Making the Shelf Work for You: How Shelf Dimensions and Brand Types Influence the Shelf Placement Effect on Product Performance
papers.authors: Kristopher O. Keller, Arjen van Lin
papers.abstract: This study examines how vertical and horizontal shelf position and shelf space affect product sales, and how these effects vary across brand types and shelf dimensions. Using sales data and detailed planogram changes from a leading convenience-store retailer, the analysis distinguishes primary NBs (market-leading national brands), secondary NBs (other nationally distributed brands), and PLs (private labels), and compares tall versus short and wide versus narrow shelves. On tall shelves, primary and secondary NBs perform best between the middle and top, whereas vertical position has little effect for PLs. On short shelves, NBs perform better toward the top and bottom, while PLs tend to perform better near the top. On wide shelves, primary NBs perform best slightly left of center, while horizontal position has little effect for secondary NBs and PLs. On narrow shelves, primary NBs perform best near the center, PLs left of center, and secondary NBs show only modest differences across positions. More shelf space increases sales most strongly for PLs. A shelf-optimization analysis suggests substantial model-implied sales improvements from shelf rearrangement. Overall, the findings help retailers assess and justify requests for contested premium positions and shelf space by showing which brand types benefit most across shelf types.

papers.title: EXPRESS: The Relationship Between a Salesperson’s Past and Future Performance
papers.authors: Melissa Baucum, Alex R. Zablah, Nawar N. Chaker, Johannes Habel
papers.abstract: A salesperson’s past performance is widely assumed to predict their future performance, and thus often guides managerial decision-making. Contrary to that assumption, this study uncovers why and under what conditions past performance becomes a less reliable predictor of future performance. A grounded theory study in a solution-selling context reveals that recent wins generate after-sales workload that lowers the odds of converting the next lead, particularly when those wins are complex, as occurs when customer relationships are new or procurement is formalized. Analysis of seven years of CRM data covering 3,669 sales leads at a Fortune 500 firm confirms that the link between past and future wins weakens as recent wins grow in complexity. Behavioral experiments causally confirm this attenuation effect, showing recent wins reduce effort on the next lead when those wins are complex. Finally, a single-dataset meta-analysis offers convergent evidence for workload as the underlying mechanism, revealing the relationship also weakens when workload is decoupled from winning and rooted in organizational change instead. For managers, these findings imply that using past performance to guide forecasting, quota setting, and coaching risks suboptimal decisions. They also underscore the importance of resourcing salespeople to balance after-sales responsibilities with new business development.
